A Simbu-szerocsoport vírusai elsősorban kérődzőket, különösen szarvasmarhákat, juhokat és kecskéket fertőznek meg. https://prwire.com.au/pr/130184/internat.text: Home Contacts Announcements About Us Home Contacts Announcements About Us International Rights Groups Raise Alarm Over Freedom of Religion and Expression in South Korea Announcement posted by SCJ Sydney 08 Aug 2026 SEOUL, South Korea, 7 August 2026 — Human Rights Without Frontiers (HRWF), together with CAP Liberté de Conscience (CAP LC), which has accredited ECOSOC status at the United Nations, FOREF, CESNUR and Bitter Winter, held a press conference today at the Seoul Foreign Correspondents' Club on Freedom of Religion or Belief and Freedom of Expression in South Korea. The issues addressed included concerns about the treatment of elderly religious leaders in pretrial detention, including questions of proportionality, humanitarian considerations, and due process. The organizations called on South Korean authorities to review the detention of 95-year-old Shincheonji Chairman Lee Man-hee and to ensure that the legal and administrative response to religious minorities remains neutral, proportionate, and consistent with South Korea's international human-rights obligations, including with respect to 83-year-old Mrs. Hak-ja Han Moon of the Family Federation. The issues discussed today form part of a broader pattern of Freedom of Religion or Belief concerns in South Korea. Concerns have also persisted regarding Segero Church in Busan, which has reportedly continued to face harassment and official scrutiny even after Pastor Son Hyun-bo was released from detention. Reporting has also raised questions about conscientious objection, public hostility toward a mosque project in Daegu, and religious accommodation in educational settings. Over the past decades, HRWF has documented the imprisonment of hundreds of Jehovah's Witnesses in South Korea as conscientious objectors, and although alternative civilian service was later introduced, critics maintain that it has been implemented in a punitive manner rather than as a genuine rights-respecting alternative, notably because it requires 36 months of service in correctional facilities, twice the length of regular military service. Recent court decisions have also upheld key features of that system against constitutional challenge. Opening the conference, Hans Noot , Associate Director of HRWF, said the issues at stake "lie at the heart of democratic society," warning that when religious communities are stigmatized, peaceful gatherings are restricted, and dissent is treated as a problem to be contained, the consequences "extend far beyond any single group or case." He said the conference was not about defending any one theology or movement, but about "defending a principle: that fundamental rights apply equally to all." Thierry Valle , President of CAP Liberté de Conscience, addressed the legality of Chairman Lee's detention under international law. Referring to South Korea's ratification of the International Covenant on Civil and Political Rights in 1990 and the Convention against Torture in 1995, he questioned whether placing a 95-year-old in pretrial detention is consistent with those obligations. He stressed that the presumption of innocence must prevail over any presumption of guilt. There are alternative more proportionate and more humane measures respecting the presumption of innocence and human dignity in democratic countries. And he cited precedents including Cardinal Joseph Zen's 2022 release on bail in Hong Kong and Vietnam's decision to place Buddhist Patriarch Thich Quang Do under house arrest rather than in prison. Michael Langhans , Executive Director of FOREF Germany, presented a legal analysis questioning whether pretrial detention for Chairman Lee of the Shincheonji Church was necessary given evidence already sufficient for an indictment, and whether that evidence was gathered neutrally rather than through a narrative framing the defendant's community as a "sect" or "cult." He argued that the case raises a broader question for lawmakers: whether measures meant to protect fair elections can be applied without nullifying the constitutionally and internationally guaranteed right to freedom of religion. Márk Nemes , Deputy Director of CESNUR, shared his thoughts on the effects of ongoing persecution and its possible ramifications for minority faiths. He noted three recent scholarly investigations conducted in selected Shincheonji congregations in Europe, Argentina, and Australia, each finding worrisome increase in hostility toward the otherwise peaceful and cooperative religious movement. He stressed that Shincheonji is not simply a South Korean minority church but a global religious movement with congregations worldwide. The disproportionate persecution in South Korea affects the lives of those congregants abroad, whose freedoms for expressing and practicing faith, enshrined in ICCPR Articles 18 and 19, are inalienable rights and must be considered during this current process. Massimo Introvigne , Managing Director of CESNUR and Editor-in-Chief of Bitter Winter, said South Korea "has crossed a worrying line" by arresting Chairman Lee, arguing that international standards such as the Mandela Rules would call for house arrest rather than imprisonment for a 95-year-old accused of a non-violent offence. He said the charges, tied to ordinary political participation by members of a religious minority, "appear legally and conceptually overstretched," and warned that the case fits a broader pattern of pressure against minority faiths in the country. The organizations called on South Korean authorities, the media, and the international community to examine these developments with close attention to due process, proportionality, and the equal protection of fundamental rights, and made further documentation available to support continued reporting. At the conclusion of the press conference, the scholars in attendance signed an official letter calling on the Government of the Republic of Korea to immediately release Chairman Lee from custody. Media Contact Human Rights Without Frontiers (HRWF) intern1@hrwf.org HRWF YouTube Note: The full proceedings of the Press Conference can be watched on HRWF YouTube Additional Articles Link here in English and Korean 2. Speakers and Organising Institutions Hans Noot Hans Noot holds a Master's degree in Organizational Behavior from Brigham Young University. Over a career spanning more than three decades, he has directed international educational and civil-society programmes across the Netherlands, Belgium, Poland, Ireland, the Czech Republic, the Balkans, and Eastern Europe. He currently serves as Associate Director and a Board Member of Human Rights Without Frontiers (HRWF) and as Director of the Gerard Noodt Foundation for Freedom of Religion or Belief. A widely published commentator on freedom of religion or belief, he regularly represents his organisations before international institutions and policymakers, and his written work is cited across a range of human-rights and religious-freedom publications. Human Rights Without Frontiers (HRWF) Human Rights Without Frontiers International (HRWF Int'l) is a leading non-profit association dedicated to shaping European and international policy in ways that strengthen democracy, uphold the rule of law, and protect human rights globally. Its influence extends across a robust network of associated member organisations spanning Denmark, France, Greece, Iraq, Italy, Japan, Moldova, Norway, Pakistan, Romania, Russia, South Korea, Turkey, Ukraine, the United Kingdom, and the United States. Since its inception, the organisation has been guided by Executive Director Willy Fautré, a respected and long-standing human rights activist with decades of experience on the international stage. HRWF Int'l conducts rigorous research, field missions, analysis, and monitoring of a wide range of human rights concerns in countries around the world, drawing on an extensive international network of correspondents who provide the NGO with reliable, first-hand information from the ground. Thierry Valle Thierry Valle has built a career of more than two decades in international human-rights advocacy, with a particular focus on freedom of conscience and freedom of religion or belief. He has lectured extensively on these subjects at conferences and academic and policy venues around the world, and has represented his organisation in formal submissions and oral interventions before the United Nations Human Rights Council and European Union institutions. He currently serves as President of CAP Liberté de Conscience, an organisation holding special consultative status with the UN Economic and Social Council (ECOSOC), and is recognised within the field as an experienced voice on the legal and policy frameworks that protect freedom of conscience internationally. CAP LC Coordination des Associations et des Particuliers pour la Liberté de Conscience CAP Freedom of Conscience is a respected secular European NGO holding United Nations Consultative Status, established in 1995 and dedicated to defending the fundamental Right of Freedom of Religion and Belief. It plays an active role in combating all forms of discrimination based on religion or belief, alerting European and international bodies and driving meaningful policy engagement on these issues. CAP Freedom of Conscience carefully collects testimonies of discrimination and human rights violations affecting religious or belief communities, disseminating them to international bodies in order to raise awareness, inform decision-makers, and generate vital debate on the protection of Freedom of Religion and Belief. As a member of the European Federation for Freedom of Belief (FOB) and the European Network of Religion and Belief (ENORB), and as a participant in the Civil Society Platform of Fundamental Rights created by the EU Fundamental Rights Agency, CAP Freedom of Conscience is firmly embedded within the leading European networks shaping the future of religious freedom. Michael Langhans Michael Langhans is a German legal expert specialising in family and child-custody law, with particular expertise in cases requiring family-court psychological assessments. A graduate of the University of Augsburg, he studied under former German Federal Constitutional Court Justice Johannes Masing, building a legal career on complex custody and family-law disputes before extending his expertise into freedom of religion or belief. He now serves as Executive Director of FOREF Germany, the newly established German section of the Forum for Religious Freedom Europe, leading its legal and advocacy work in the country. FOREF Germany FOREF Germany is the newly established German section of the Forum for Religious Freedom Europe (FOREF), an independent, secular human-rights organisation with roots stretching back to 1998. Launched in December 2025 through a partnership between FOREF co-founder Peter Zoehrer and German legal expert Michael Langhans, FOREF Germany brings deep, specialised legal expertise in family and custody law directly to the defence of religious minorities in the country. With the relaunch of its German-language platform in March 2026, the organisation is positioned to become a leading voice for freedom of religion or belief in one of Europe's most influential nations. Prof. Massimo Introvigne Massimo Introvigne is an Italian sociologist of religion, author, and intellectual-property attorney whose scholarship spans more than four decades. He has authored approximately 70 books and over 100 academic articles in the sociology of religion, and is widely regarded as one of the field's foremost international authorities — described by fellow academics as "one of the major names in the study of new religions" and as being "among the world's leading scholars of new religious movements." He co-founded CESNUR (Center for Studies on New Religions) in 1988 and has served as its Managing Director since, and is also Editor-in-Chief of the daily magazine Bitter Winter. His research has been presented before academic conferences, parliamentary bodies, and international organisations including the OSCE. CESNUR Center for Studies on New Religions CESNUR, the Center for Studies on New Religions, was founded in 1988 and is recognised as the oldest scholarly organisation devoted exclusively to the academic study of new religious movements and religious pluralism. In more than three decades of activity, it has convened scholars from leading universities across Europe, North America, and Asia, with over 1,000 papers presented at its international conferences and seminars — many going on to appear in leading international journals, alongside CESNUR's own peer-reviewed Journal of CESNUR. The organisation is directed by Managing Director Massimo Introvigne, one of the most widely published scholars in the sociology of religion, and also publishes Bitter Winter, a daily magazine on religious liberty and human rights that is regularly cited by journalists and policymakers researching religious minorities worldwide. Bitter Winter Bitter Winter was launched in May 2018 as a pioneering online magazine dedicated to religious liberty and human rights in China, published by CESNUR, the Center for Studies on New Religions, headquartered in Torino, Italy. Since December 1, 2020, Bitter Winter has expanded with a dedicated international section covering religious liberty worldwide, and continues to grow its coverage into new countries and emerging issues with each passing year. Being published by CESNUR gives Bitter Winter a particularly sharp, well-informed lens on religious liberty issues connected with new religious movements, while its broader mission ensures thorough coverage of all forms of religion and belief — making it an increasingly trusted and cited resource for readers following religious freedom developments around the globe. Dr. Márk Nemes Dr. Márk Nemes is a Hungarian historian and philosopher specialising in the theory of religion. He completed his PhD in Philosophy at the University of Szeged's Málnási Bartók György Doctoral School in 2025, and was awarded the prestigious Hungarian National Eötvös Scholarship in recognition of his research. He holds a full-time researcher and research-coordinator position at the Hungarian Academy of Arts' Research Institute for Art Theory and Methodology in Budapest, where his work explores the intersections of art, aesthetics, and religiosity. In 2025 he was appointed Deputy Director of CESNUR, and he is a co-founder of CESAR (Central European Symposium for the Academic Study of Religion), a research network supporting early-career scholars of religion across Central and Eastern Europe. CESNUR Center for Studies on New Religions CESNUR, the Center for Studies on New Religions, was founded in 1988 and is recognised as the oldest scholarly organisation devoted exclusively to the academic study of new religious movements and religious pluralism. In more than three decades of activity, it has convened scholars from leading universities across Europe, North America, and Asia, with over 1,000 papers presented at its international conferences and seminars — many going on to appear in leading international journals, alongside CESNUR's own peer-reviewed Journal of CESNUR. The organisation is directed by Managing Director Massimo Introvigne, one of the most widely published scholars in the sociology of religion, and also publishes Bitter Winter, a daily magazine on religious liberty and human rights that is regularly cited by journalists and policymakers researching religious minorities worldwide.

http://www.jpost.com/israel-news/article.text: Israel Police on Thursday morning imposed a gag order on details of the investigation into the disappearance of Mali and Liel Yahalomi in Austria.A judge approved a request by YALACH, the National Economic Crimes Unit in the police's Lahav 433 National Crimes Unit, to prohibit the publication of any details from the investigation.Concern continues to grow for Yahalomi womenThe Yahalomis have been missing in Vienna since Friday and failed to board their scheduled return flight from Prague on Tuesday night, as Austrian police continue investigating their disappearance on Wednesday.The two did not arrive for their return flight, which was scheduled to depart Prague at 9:45 p.m.According to the information available, the vacation apartment where they had been staying in Vienna was found empty of their belongings. Austrian police, the Israeli Embassy, and the city's Chabad community have reported that there are still no leads in the case.Earlier, it was reported that police were examining all possibilities after reviewing videos and other footage showing the two leaving their hotel room on their own.At a later stage, their phones were located in the vicinity of a Vienna train station. Their trail has since gone cold, raising suspicions that they may have been abducted.Modi'in police questioned other members of the family, including the missing woman's son and daughter, her brother, and others, who said they last spoke with their mother and sister on Friday.Mother's involvement in embezzlement scheme revealed, Bank of Jerusalem shares plummetIsrael Police on Wednesday examined claims that the mother, a senior employee at a bank, was allegedly behind an embezzlement scheme. That suspicion was ruled out in the initial investigation. Since no bloodstains or bodies have been found, suspicion has grown that the two deliberately fled and are currently in hiding for reasons that remain unclear.According to reports, Bank of Jerusalem CEO Yair Kaplan told staff on Thursday that he was aware of reports concerning Yahalomi's disappearance.“We understand that an incident such as this raises concerns and uncertainty,” Kaplan wrote.“It should be emphasized that, apart from the fact that she is an employee of the bank, no connection has been found between the incident and the bank,” he added. Kaplan also reminded employees that the investigation was subject to a gag order and that information about it must not be shared.Bank of Jerusalem's share price fell as much as 12.4% in Thursday trading, according to Tel Aviv Stock Exchange data, before recovering most of the loss.Amir Rudnik, Mali Yahalomi's brother-in-law, spoke to 103FM on Wednesday and shared the latest information available to him about the disappearance."We don't have much information. We have a contact person at the Foreign Ministry situation room, and we also have a representative from the consulate in Vienna," Rudnik said. "They've started checking, but so far there's nothing. They arrived in Vienna from Prague by train, spent the night between Friday and Saturday at an apartment hotel in Vienna, and their Google account shows that the phone was last seen in the area of a train station in Vienna."Rudnik said the two had been on a regular mother-daughter trip, and that they come from a “normal, close-knit family.”“We have a family WhatsApp group, we're in touch every day, and every member of the family shares experiences and photos. She's 50, and she's a banker. Her daughter is 23. Mali also has an older son. We know that the return flight, which was yesterday, was from Prague to Ben-Gurion Airport. They were supposed to return to Prague and fly back home in the evening,” he said.The Israeli Embassy in Vienna issued an appeal on Wednesday for help locating the two Israeli citizens, mother and daughter Mali and Liel Yahalomi, after contact with them was lost on Friday, August 7. In a post published on social media, the embassy included photographs of the two and asked the public to share the notice and help locate them.The Yahalomi family in Israel issued a brief statement on Thursday, reiterating that there was no connection between the disappearance and Bank of Jerusalem's share price. The family stressed that it would not acknowledge any information about the case unless it came directly from official sources.Sarah Ben-Nun contributed to this report.

https://telex.hu/kulfold/2026/08/27/nepa.text: Menü Kereső Közel 1500 eltűntet, köztük 800 külföldi állampolgárt keresnek a villámárvíz után Nepálban és Tibetben Külföld Iván-Nagy Szilvia Állítsd be a Telexet megbízható forrásnak! Beállítom Közel 1500 embert, köztük 800 külföldi állampolgárt keresnek a hatóságok Nepálban és Tibetben, miután villámárvíz öntötte el Nepált és Tibetet – közölte a Reuters csütörtökön. A rendőrség arra számít, hogy a halálos áldozatok száma a 165-öt is meghaladhatja. Nepálban a rendőrség és a turisztikai szervek szerint a 826 eltűnt ember közül csaknem 600 külföldi állampolgár van, több mint 24 országból. A Reuters tájékoztatása szerint az eltűnt turisták között 177 indiai, 63 amerikai, 34 ausztrál, 33 brit és 25 kanadai állampolgárról tudnak. Tibet Gyirong megyéjében 558 eltűntről számolt be a kínai állami televízió csütörtökön. Közülük 260-an külföldi állampolgárok. A magyar Külügyminisztérium tájékoztatása szerint két magyar állampolgár is eltűnt a szerdai villámárvízben , őket eltűntként jelentették a konzulátus, illetve a Külügyminisztérium felé. A nepáli tisztviselők első jelentései szerint a térségben történt földrengés okozhatta egy gleccser alsó részének összeomlását, ami kiválthatta az áradásokat, ám az Egyesült Államok Földtani Szolgálata (USGS) szerint a kezdetben 4,4-es erősségűnek jelentett földrengés valójában a gleccserből származó sziklák és jég összeomlása során felszabaduló szeizmikus energia volt, amelyet törmelékár követett. Az áldozatok közül sokan a Manszarovar-tóhoz és a mellette emelkedő Kajlás-hegyhez tartó zarándokúton haladtak. A tibeti helyszínt többek között a hinduk és a buddhisták is szent helyként tisztelik: úgy tartják, a hegy Síva lakhelye. Az amerikai külügyminisztérium katasztrófaelhárítási tanácsadót küld a térségbe, és 500 ezer dollár értékű segítséget nyújt, az ENSZ pedig ellátmányt és személyi támogatást küld az érintett nepáli közösségekhez – közölte António Guterres ENSZ-főtitkár. A Nepálon és Tibeten is keresztül folyó Bhotekoshi szerda reggel lépett ki medréből , a hirtelen jött árvíz több falut elöntött és az infrastruktúrát is megrongálta. Nepálban házakat, utakat, hidakat és energetikai létesítményeket sodort el a víz. A Bhotekoshi folyó tavaly is kiöntött, az árvíz akkor kilenc ember életét követelte, és elsodorta a Nepált és Kínát összekötő Barátság-hidat. https://www.mainlinemedianews.com/2026/0.text: Germany’s Interior Minister Alexander Dobrindt speaks to the media during a press conference in Berlin on Tuesday, Sept. 1, 2026, about the attempted attack on Leipzig/Halle Airport last month with a drone loaded with explosives.(AP Photo/Ebrahim Noroozi) By Associated Press PUBLISHED: September 1, 2026 at 11:51 AM EDT | UPDATED: September 1, 2026 at 4:14 PM EDT Getting your Trinity Audio player ready... By GEIR MOULSON, Associated Press BERLIN (AP) — The German government on Tuesday blamed Russia for an attempted attack at Leipzig/Halle Airport last month using a drone laden with explosives , and announced that it would shut down a Russian consulate among other measures. The drone was found near a Ukrainian plane on Aug. 4 and the device was defused. German officials said at the time that the incident posed a new level of danger. Moscow has been widely accused by Western officials of running a campaign of sabotage and disruption with the aim of undermining support for Ukraine and destabilizing European nations. Minister says evidence points to a familiar pattern German Interior Minister Alexander Dobrindt said authorities found elements such as the drone configuration, components, explosives and detonator that are “known to us from other Russian hybrid operations and its war against Ukraine.” He said the device pointed to “a high degree of technical expertise” and painstaking planning, but carrying out the plan appears to have been left to “low-level” agents. Dobrindt told reporters that intelligence points to “people being involved who acted on behalf of Russian state entities,” though he didn’t specify which ones. “Taken together, the police investigations, the pattern and intelligence findings prove a Russian responsibility for the attempted attack at Leipzig airport.” Germany will shut a Russian consulate Foreign Minister Johann Wadephul said that “with the attempted attack in Leipzig, the Russian leadership decided deliberately to do significant damage again to our already massively burdened bilateral relationship.” He said the Russian consulate in Bonn will be closed effective Sept. 18. The Russian House cultural center in Berlin also will be closed, though that may take some time. Germany will propose the addition of more people from Russia to European Union sanctions lists “in the context of hybrid attacks,” step up entry controls for people from Russia and increase “pressure on the shadow fleet,” a reference to tankers suspected of shipping Russian oil in violation of international sanctions, Wadephul said. The EU has sanctioned hundreds of “shadow fleet” ships. The Russian ambassador was summoned to the Foreign Ministry in Berlin. Wadephul later told ARD television that “Germany can at any time show a stronger reaction, (but) that is not necessary at this point.” Russian Foreign Ministry spokesperson Maria Zakharova said there would be a “fitting response” to the planned closures, Russian state news agency Tass reported. She rejected claims of Russian involvement in the attempted drone attack, calling them a “far-fetched and contrived pretext” for Berlin to escalate tensions and arguing that “as usual, no convincing or serious evidence has been presented whatsoever.” Around 200 incidents blamed on Russia Leipzig/Halle is a major hub for international freight and for providing support to Ukraine. The planes that regularly use it include Ukrainian Antonov transport aircraft. It is also home to NATO’s Strategic Airlift International Solution, or SALIS, which is currently operational almost every day in delivering equipment to NATO battle groups along its eastern flank from Finland to Romania and supporting EU and alliance nation missions. In 2024, an incendiary device ignited at a logistics center at the airport and set fire to a freight container before it could be loaded onto a cargo plane, part of a plot that Western security officials suspect was organized by Russian intelligence. The Associated Press has tracked around 200 incidents of sabotage and malign activity across Europe blamed on Russia by Western officials since the invasion of Ukraine. That includes organizing plots to set fire to warehouses , launching drones and trying to kill enemies abroad as well as stealing defense technology and carrying out cyberattacks on critical European infrastructure. In May, Russian President Vladimir Putin responded to the AP findings and said Moscow is not waging a sabotage campaign against Europe. He demanded that AP “name one proven fact.” Russia has faced many packages of EU sanctions The EU has slapped almost two dozen packages of sanctions on Russia over its war in Ukraine, targeting roughly 3,000 people and entities. EU foreign ministers will meet in Ireland Wednesday. European allies rallied around Germany after Tuesday’s announcement. NATO Secretary-General Mark Rutte said in a post on X that he had spoken with Chancellor Friedrich Merz and “NATO stands in full solidarity with Germany after the Russian hybrid attack in Leipzig.” In mid-August, the German Cabinet approved plans to give the country’s intelligence services broader powers for actions such as disabling sabotage and hacking attempts. The planned reform, which had been in the works for months, still requires parliamentary approval. Prosecutors said Monday they launched an investigation based on suspicions of the “participation of foreign intelligence activities against the Republic of Poland,” without elaborating on what country might be responsible. They said the fire in Skarżysko-Kamienna destroyed warehouse facilities and caused damage estimated at at least 15 million zlotys ($4 million). https://www.dw.com/en/pakistan-says-stri.text: Skip to content Skip to main menu Skip to more DW sites https://p.dw.com/p/5MwiS Taliban officials accused Pakistan of targeting civilians Image: Shafiullah Kakar/AP Photo/dpa/picture alliance Advertisement Pakistan conducted airstrikes on northeastern Afghanistan on Monday on what Pakistan's Ministry of Information described as suicide bomber training facilities. It was the first Pakistani strike of its kind on Afghan territory since June, and followed soon after an attack targeting Pakistani police across the border in Kohat . The uneasy neighbors reported seemingly conflicting casualty tolls. What were the conflicting accounts on the strikes? Pakistan's Ministry of Information and Broadcasting claimed online that the attacks had targeted terrorist training sites in Afghanistan with "precision and accuracy." "Three targets were destroyed with precision including a Suicide Bombers training markaz [station], killing 28 terrorists alongside multiple suicide bombers. Large quantities of weapons and ammunition ... were also destroyed," the Ministry said. The Taliban government in Kabul, meanwhile, claimed that three people were killed as it accused Pakistan of bombarding "civilian homes." Afghanistan's deputy government spokesperson Hamdullah Fitrat said that the strikes took place in the Kunar and Paktika provinces. Fitrat wrote on X that one strike hit at around 3:00 am Monday (2230 UTC, Sunday) in Kunar's Nurgal district and "completely destroyed" a house, adding that three people were killed and four other members of the family were wounded. He said that two locations were also hit in the Paktika province, claiming that a shop and an unoccupied house were destroyed. Neither side's assertions on the details of and casualties from the strikes could be immediately verified. The latest strikes threaten to shatter three months of relative calm Image: Shafiullah Kakar/AP Photo/dpa/picture alliance Strikes follow last week's militant attack in Pakistan The reported strikes come after a suicide bombing and a 20-hour gun battle between militants and police on Friday, which took place at a district police headquarters compound in the Pakistani city of Kohat, situated near the Afghan border. At least 31 people, including 16 police officers, were killed in the attack. Ittehad-ul-Mujahideen Pakistan, a local militant group linked to the jihadist group Tehreek-i-Taliban Pakistan (TTP), claimed responsibility for the attack. The Afghanistan-Pakistan conflict Relations between Afghanistan and Pakistan have been tense since the Taliban returned to power in 2021. The latest strikes threaten to shatter three months of relative calm after former South Asian allies engaged in their worst clashes in years in February. Pakistan declared that month that it was in an "open war” with Afghanistan , following a rise in militant attacks on civilians and security forces inside Pakistan. Afghanistan launched retaliatory strikes after Pakistan carried out airstrikes inside Afghan territory and the cross-border fighting has since claimed the lives of hundreds of people. Pakistan last mounted deadly airstrikes in Afghanistan in June. Islamabad accuses Afghanistan of sheltering militant groups which launch attacks inside Pakistan's territory. Main among these is the TTP, often referred to as the Pakistani Taliban and Baloch separatist groups from the border areas. The Taliban has dismissed ​the allegations, saying that militancy in Pakistan is an internal problem. Are Pakistan and Afghanistan heading for war? Play Video Article content Ukraine’s state railway operator Ukrzaliznytsia said a drone was detected and an evacuation order was issued 15 minutes before the strike, BBC News reported. “Shortly before the locomotive was hit at the Ukrainian-Polish border, a diplomatic train was at Yagodyn station,” Ukrzaliznytsia said in a statement, per AFP. “There were, among others, security advisers from several EU member states and former European leaders on board, including former U.K. prime minister Boris Johnson. Sign In or Create an Account or View more offers Article content Russian forces launched an attack near the Yahodyn checkpoint along Ukraine’s border with Poland on Sept. 13. A nearby gas station was reportedly damaged in the strike, according to local authorities. “Russia’s barbaric strikes near the Ukrainian-Polish border in Yahodyn are… pic.twitter.com/4wJuladGYM — The Kyiv Independent (@KyivIndependent) September 13, 2026 BoJo slams Putin’s ‘warped logic’ Johnson and the European officials were reportedly passing through the station on their way back from a conference in Kyiv. “I don’t know what warped logic drove Putin to blow up a stationary Ukrainian locomotive on the Polish border this morning,” Johnson said in a post on X Sunday. “What we can say for sure is that this is the kind of random and senseless attack Ukrainians are enduring every day — even on civilian railways.” A train’s engine was hit in the strike with no casualties reported. At a nearby gas station, two trucks were hit and caught fire, a spokesperson for the Polish Interior Ministry told AFP. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said Moscow had “deliberately” struck the locomotive. “It is precisely to prevent these strikes from spreading further into Europe that Ukrainian men and women fight every day, give their lives and do not allow the aggression to expand,” Zelenskyy said via AFP. Poland also denounced the strikes, including another near a frontier checkpoint, as an “escalation” in the war. Calgary Sun Headline News Get the latest headlines, breaking news and columns. Play Video Russian escalation expected to continue But the strikes came as U.S. President Donald Trump called on Zelenskyy to halt attacks on Russian refineries, saying it was causing a shortage of diesel fuel and “there are plenty of other targets.” Ukraine has increasingly targeted Russian oil refineries in a bid to hurt Russia’s war effort. European nations are meanwhile worried by what they say is increased Russian-orchestrated sabotage acts on their soil. Poland has been one of Ukraine’s main allies and with Ukrainian airspace closed, trains to Poland have been one of the main routes out of the war-torn country and are being used by refugees. Poland’s Prime Minister Donald Tusk chaired an emergency meeting in Warsaw following the strikes, warning he expected Russia to escalate the war “in the coming weeks.” He added: “We cannot exclude that the escalation will also affect our territory… I hope not.” Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy speaks during a joint press conference with Lithuania’s President Gitanas Nauseda and Polish President Karol Nawrocki, at the Presidential palace in Vilnius, Lithuania, Sunday, Jan. 25, 2026. Article content Russian attacks also killed at least two people on Sunday in the frontline city of Kramatorsk. Twenty people, including two children, were also wounded in a second day of attacks on the southern port city of Odesa, Ukrainian officials said. The Kremlin, meanwhile, said negotiations with Ukraine and the United States on the war could take place in October. “We do not rule out such a possibility; we are talking about the foreseeable future,” Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov told journalists, cited by Russia’s Ria and Tass news agencies. Several rounds of negotiations have failed, while U.S.-led efforts stalled during the Middle East war. In an interview released on Saturday, Zelenskyy said he would be willing to meet Putin at the G20 summit in Miami in December. But Peskov said that was “impossible,” speaking to AFP in New Delhi on Saturday, repeating Moscow’s demand that a meeting could only take place in the Russian capital. — With files from AFP. Greece: Thousands flood Athens streets in education protest Copy/paste the link below: Copy Copy/paste the article video embed link below: Copy Updated: 21/10/2026 - 23:02 GMT+2 Thousands of protesters marched through Athens on Wednesday 21 October, demanding greater investment in education. Crowds filled the streets of the capital, waving banners, chanting slogans and beating drums as they made their way past the Greek parliament. … More Students, teachers and public-sector workers marched through central Athens on Wednesday, demanding more funding for education , smaller classes , better facilities and affordable student housing . ADVERTISEMENT ADVERTISEMENT Aerial footage showed crowds filling major streets as protesters made their way from the University of Athens towards the Greek Parliament . Some banners written in French reflected the Greek protesters' solidarity with , and inspiration from, recent student demonstrations in France . Organisers presented the march as part of a broader European movement calling for better-funded education , affordable housing and relief from rising living costs . Police officers , including riot police carrying shields, accompanied the march and blocked nearby roads . Some shops and cafés closed their shutters as a precaution. The demonstration was part of a nationwide protest movement , with rallies also held in Thessaloniki, Patras, Larissa and Crete . Police estimated that around 10,000 people took part in Athens and its suburbs, although organisers claimed a higher turnout . Some demonstrators had camped overnight outside Parliament , calling for rent controls , greater housing support and more investment in public education . The rally ended peacefully shortly before 2pm, reflecting mounting pressure on the Greek government to address education funding and the financial difficulties facing students.
